summary: Republishes PKCS #12 version 1.1, a syntax for transferring personal identity information such as private keys and certificates. It moves change control from RSA Laboratories to the IETF.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a standard locked bag for carrying your private keys and ID certificates from one device to another.

questions: what is inside a pkcs12 file
subtitle: The PFX file format for carrying private keys and certificates between machines, now under IETF change control.

tldr.problem: A user needs to move a set of personal identity information, such as private keys and certificates, from one platform to another safely.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #12 defines a PFX container that holds typed bags of keys, certificates, CRLs and secrets, with encryption by public key or password and integrity protection by signature or password-based MAC.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7292 republishes PKCS #12 v1.1 so that change control moves from RSA Laboratories to the IETF. It notes the password privacy key method is deprecated and has been updated by RFC 9579 and RFC 9879.

today: RFC 7292 is an Informational RFC and has been updated by RFC 9579 and RFC 9879. Its own text deprecates the Appendix B method for password privacy mode in favor of PKCS #5 v2.1, and it says enhancements preserving backward compatibility were expected in an upcoming IETF Standards Track document.

sections.title: What PKCS #12 Is and Why It Is an RFC
sections.content:
PKCS #12 describes a transfer syntax for personal identity information, including private keys, certificates, miscellaneous secrets and extensions. Machines, applications, browsers and Internet kiosks that support it let a user import, export and use a single set of personal identity information.

RFC 7292 is a republication of PKCS #12 v1.1 from RSA Laboratories. Publishing it as an RFC transfers change control to the IETF. The body is taken directly from the original, except the Security Considerations, and references were updated. Changes from version 1 include added hash algorithms, the incorporation of Technical Corrigendum #1, and a recommendation to stop using the Appendix B technique for password privacy mode in favor of PKCS #5 v2.1.
sections.plainLanguage: People already used this bag format. This note hands the job of looking after it over to a new group of caretakers, with a few small fixes.

sections.title: Privacy and Integrity Modes
sections.content:
There are four combinations of two privacy modes (encryption) and two integrity modes (tamper protection).

  • Public-key privacy: the data is enveloped with a trusted encryption public key of a known destination platform.
  • Password privacy: the data is encrypted with a symmetric key derived from a user name and a privacy password.
  • Public-key integrity: a digital signature over the contents, made with the source platform's private signature key.
  • Password integrity: a Message Authentication Code (MAC) derived from a secret integrity password.

All combinations are allowed. In general the public-key modes are preferable from a security viewpoint, but they are not always possible. For example, if the destination platform is not known at export time, public-key privacy mode cannot be used. The integrity wrapper goes around everything, the reverse of the order in many protocols, so that as much information as possible is protected.
sections.plainLanguage: You can lock the bag with a special key made for the person getting it, or with a password. You can also add a seal that shows if anyone tampered with it, also using a key or a password.

sections.title: The PFX Structure and Bag Types
sections.content:
The top-level PFX holds a version (which must be v3), an authSafe ContentInfo, and an optional MacData that is present only in password integrity mode. In public-key integrity mode the ContentInfo is signedData; in password mode it is data.

The authSafe contains an AuthenticatedSafe, a sequence of ContentInfo values. Each is plaintext, password-encrypted or public-key enveloped, and holds a SafeContents, which is a sequence of SafeBag entries. Each SafeBag has an object identifier, a value and optional attributes such as a friendly name or local key identifier.

Six bag types are defined: KeyBag (one PKCS #8 private key), PKCS8ShroudedKeyBag (one encrypted private key), CertBag (X.509 or SDSI certificate), CRLBag (X.509 CRL), SecretBag (one miscellaneous secret) and a nested SafeContents. The set can be extended in future versions.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a big suitcase with several smaller bags inside. Some bags hold keys, some hold ID cards, and some hold other secrets, and each bag has a label saying what is inside.

sections.title: Creating and Importing a PFX
sections.content:
To create a PFX, make one or more SafeContents values and wrap each in its own ContentInfo: plain Data, password-based EncryptedData or public-key EnvelopedData. String the ContentInfo values together into an AuthenticatedSafe and BER-encode it into a Data ContentInfo. Then add integrity protection: either wrap it in SignedData, or compute an HMAC with SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224 or SHA-512/256.

Importing reverses the steps. An application should ignore object identifiers it does not recognize, and may alert the user to them. It should take care when an imported item would overwrite an existing local one, and it may be appropriate to ask the user what to do.

The multi-part design lets an implementer, for example, leave already-shrouded keys without a second layer of encryption, since the RFC says such super-encryption can limit a product's exportability.
sections.plainLanguage: To pack, you put things in bags, put the bags in a suitcase, and add a lock or seal. To unpack, you do it backwards, and you ask before replacing something you already own.

sections.title: Deriving Keys from Passwords
sections.content:
Appendix B describes a method that uses a hash function, a password, salt and an iteration count to produce pseudorandom bits. An ID byte says what the bits are for: 1 for an encryption key, 2 for an initial value, 3 for a MAC integrity key. Passwords are treated as BMPStrings with a NULL terminator, so each character takes 2 bytes, big-endian.

The RFC says this method is not recommended and is deprecated for new use in password privacy mode, where PKCS #5 v2.1 should be used instead (PBES2 with PBKDF2). It is retained for backwards compatibility with PKCS #12 v1.0, and it is still used to derive the MAC key in password integrity mode. The RFC recommends that future PFX definitions replace the existing MacData with a MAC based on the PKCS #5 PBMAC1 scheme.

The iteration count is recommended to be 1024 or more, and ideally the salt is as long as the hash output and made of random bits.
sections.plainLanguage: A short password gets mixed up many, many times with some random sprinkles (salt) to make a strong lock. The old mixing recipe still works but people are told to use a newer one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Password-based cryptography is limited in the security it can provide, particularly because off-line password search is possible against the methods in this document. Salt and an iteration count raise the cost of an attack, but passwords must be chosen well, following guidelines such as NIST SP 800-61-1, and protected if stored.

When choosing a salt, the recommendations in Section 4 of PKCS #5 2.1 apply. Ideally the salt is as long as the output of the hash function and consists of randomly generated data. Section 3.2 adds that it can be unwise to move private keys without physical protection in password privacy mode.
sections.plainLanguage: A password lock can be tried over and over by a patient thief, so pick a long, hard password and keep it safe.
